lesson.title: The Meter Changes What It Measures: Understanding Loading Error
lesson.summary: Loading error is the deviation between a true circuit value and what a real, finite impedance measuring instrument reports, because connecting a real voltmeter or scope probe inevitably draws a small current that the ideal circuit analysis never accounted for.
lesson.body:
Every voltage divider calculation you have done so far assumed an ideal voltmeter: a measuring instrument with infinite input resistance that draws absolutely no current and therefore cannot disturb the circuit it is connected to. This is exactly the loading effect you have already studied in the abstract, a source's output being pulled down by whatever load is attached to it. A real multimeter or oscilloscope input is that load, since it has a finite, if often large, input resistance, and loading error is simply the name for the resulting gap between the true, undisturbed value in the circuit and the value the instrument actually reports once it is connected and drawing its own small current.

A worked example makes the size of this effect concrete. Consider a voltage divider built from two 1 megohm resistors, R1 and R2, fed from a 10 volt source. Ideally, since the two resistors are equal, the output across R2 should be exactly half the input, or 5 volts. Now connect a typical digital multimeter, with an input resistance of 10 megohms, across R2 to measure that voltage. The meter's 10 megohm resistance sits electrically in parallel with the 1 megohm R2, and that parallel combination is what the divider actually sees: R2 parallel with 10 megohms works out to (1 times 10) divided by (1 plus 10), or 10 divided by 11 megohms, approximately 0.909 megohms, noticeably less than the original 1 megohm. Plugging that reduced resistance back into the divider equation, the measured output becomes 10 volts times 0.909 divided by (1 plus 0.909), which comes out to almost exactly 4.76 volts. The meter, simply by being connected, has pulled the true 5.00 volt node down to a reported 4.76 volts, an error of about 0.24 volts, or roughly 4.8 percent low, even though the meter is functioning perfectly and was never miscalibrated.

Notice what drove the size of that error: it was not that 10 megohms is a small number in any absolute sense, it is a large resistance by everyday standards, it is that 10 megohms is not overwhelmingly larger than the 1 megohm resistors already in the circuit. If the divider had instead been built from 1 kilohm resistors, the same 10 megohm meter would barely disturb it at all, since 10 megohms in parallel with 1 kilohm is nearly indistinguishable from 1 kilohm alone. This is the general rule behind loading error: it becomes significant whenever the instrument's input impedance is only modestly larger than the impedance of the circuit node being probed, and it becomes negligible when the instrument's impedance dwarfs the circuit's. That is exactly why oscilloscope probes often include a switchable 10x attenuation setting, which trades some signal amplitude for raising the effective input impedance the scope presents to the circuit, typically to around 10 megohms instead of the scope's bare 1 megohm input, reducing loading on higher impedance signal sources.

Because loading error is predictable from the circuit and the instrument's known input impedance, as the worked example above shows, it is not a random fluke, it is a systematic, repeatable bias, a distinction that matters a great deal and is picked up directly in the chapter on measurement error that follows this one.
